passage:
Pia had folded eleven paper airplanes, and every one of them had crashed.

The school's paper airplane contest was on Friday, and the plane that flew the farthest would win a shiny blue ribbon. Pia wanted that ribbon more than anything. She had given her planes long, pointed noses, wide wings, and even little paper tails, and she had decorated them with colorful stripes. They certainly looked fast. But every time she threw one, it flipped over and dove straight into the grass.

On Thursday afternoon, Pia sat on the back steps and sulked. Her little brother Teo wandered outside carrying a plain sheet of paper. He folded it in half, bent down two corners, and made two simple wings, which took him less than a minute.

"That one won't fly," Pia told him. "It doesn't even have a tail."

Teo shrugged and tossed it gently. The plane sailed across the whole yard and landed softly near the fence.

Pia stared in surprise. Then she picked up the plane and carefully turned it over in her hands. The wings were flat and even, and both sides were exactly the same. Her own planes, she realized, had been heavier on one side because of all the extra paper she had added.

"Can you show me how you did that?" she asked.

Teo grinned. "Only if I get to help with the stripes."

That evening, the two of them sat at the kitchen table and folded plane after plane. Pia kept the wings flat and the sides even, and she left off the decorations that had made her earlier planes so heavy. When she tested her new plane in the hallway, it glided all the way to the front door.

On Friday, Pia's plane did not win the blue ribbon; it came in second. But as she walked home beside Teo, she did not feel disappointed at all. She already had an idea for next year's plane, and she knew exactly who would help her build it.

choices: a boy who wins a blue ribbon at a school contest
a girl who learns from her younger brother how to make a better paper airplane
the history of paper airplane contests
a girl who decides to stop making paper airplanes
explanation: The story follows Pia as Teo shows her a simple plane and she uses his idea to build a better one.

passage:
On a summer evening, you might see small dark shapes darting through the air above a pond. Many of them are bats, out hunting for insects. Bats fly in the dark, yet they almost never bump into trees or into each other. How do they do it?

Most bats use a special skill called echolocation. As a bat flies, it makes very high squeaks and clicks, sounds so high that people cannot hear them. When a sound hits an object, such as a moth or a branch, it bounces back to the bat. This returning sound is called an echo, and the bat listens carefully to every one.

Echoes give a bat a great deal of information. If an echo comes back quickly, the object is close. If it takes longer, the object is farther away. The echoes can even tell the bat how big an insect is and in which direction it is traveling. A bat's large ears help it catch these faint sounds.

When a bat gets close to an insect, it squeaks faster and faster. Each new echo tells the bat exactly where its dinner is. Then, in a flash, the bat snatches its meal right out of the air. A single small bat can catch hundreds of insects in one night.

Bats are not the only animals that use echoes. Dolphins send out clicks to locate fish in dark or cloudy water. People have borrowed the idea, too. Ships use a tool called sonar, which sends sound waves through the water to measure the depth of the sea or to locate other ships.

So the next time you see bats at dusk, remember that they are not just flying around. They are listening their way through the night.

choices: why bats sleep during the day

explanation: Most of the passage explains echolocation and how it helps bats fly and hunt.

passage:
In 1860, the United States stretched from one ocean to another, but news traveled across it very slowly. A letter mailed in Missouri might take three weeks or more to reach California by stagecoach. People in the West wanted a faster way to hear from friends and family in the East.

That spring, a company started a bold new service called the Pony Express. Instead of slow coaches, it used riders on fast horses. The route ran nearly two thousand miles, from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. Along the way were more than 150 stations, most of them about ten to fifteen miles apart.

The system worked like a relay race. A rider galloped at top speed to the next station, where a fresh horse was waiting, saddled and ready. He swapped horses in about two minutes and raced on. After riding about seventy-five miles, he handed the mail pouch to a new rider. Riders carried the mail day and night. They rode through hot deserts, snowy mountains, and pouring rain. With this system, a letter could cross the country in about ten days.

Riders had to be small, tough, and brave. Many of them were teenagers. To save weight, letters were written on very thin paper, and sending one cost a lot of money.

Yet the Pony Express lasted only about eighteen months. In October 1861, workers finished a telegraph line that joined the East and West coasts. A message that once took ten days could now travel in minutes along the wire. Almost overnight, the riders were no longer needed, and the Pony Express shut down.

Even so, people still remember it today. The Pony Express showed how much Americans wanted to stay connected, and its riders became symbols of courage and speed.

choices: a fast mail service that crossed the country for a short time
the building of the first railroad across the country
the life of one famous Pony Express rider
explanation: The passage describes how the Pony Express worked and why it lasted only about eighteen months.

passage:
Louis Braille was born in a small village in France in 1809. When he was three years old, he was playing in his father's leather workshop and hurt his eye with a sharp tool. The eye became infected, and the infection soon spread to his other eye. By the age of five, Louis was completely blind.

Louis was a bright and curious boy, and his parents wanted him to learn. At ten, he won a place at a special school for blind children in Paris. The school had a few books for blind readers, but they were huge and heavy. Each letter was printed large and raised so that students could feel its shape with their fingers. Reading this way was very slow, and students could not easily write this way on their own.

One day, a former soldier visited the school. He showed the students a code that soldiers could read in the dark. It used raised dots pressed into paper. The code was clever, but it was also hard to use. Some words needed dozens of dots, so a reader could not feel them with one touch.

Louis could not stop thinking about the dots. For the next few years, he worked on the idea whenever he had free time. Finally, when he was only fifteen, he created a simpler system. Each letter was made from a small group of up to six dots, set in two columns of three. A fingertip could feel a whole letter at once. Louis later added patterns for numbers and even music.

At first, many teachers did not accept the new system. Some sighted adults liked the old raised letters better. But the students loved Braille's code and kept using it. In 1854, two years after Louis died, the school finally adopted it.

Today, people all over the world read braille. You may even find it on elevator buttons and signs. The idea of a curious fifteen-year-old has helped millions of people read and write on their own.
